title: Garry Tan on how YC evaluates startups: product-market fit, co-founders, fundraising, culture
summary: Garry Tan draws on Palantir, Posterous and YC to explain why founders miss product-market fit, why answering "both" is a strategic mistake, and how to read customer feedback. He also covers co-founder conflict, founder-led culture, fundraising in a tough market and why the startup ceiling keeps rising.

principles.text: Pick one path and say no to the rest; answering "both" lets competitors win each space.
principles.quote: because we chose something in between we sort of did both poorly and then we allowed our competitors to basically win in their respective spaces

principles.text: Find a narrow, underserved segment and build a much better wedge there instead of a vague broad product.
principles.quote: she started spending a lot more time with a certain segment of people so she discovered skilled nursing facilities and convalescent homes

principles.text: User feedback is worthless until money or behavior changes; people are polite and will lie to you.
principles.quote: until they're paying for something or changing a behavior that they would only do out of self-interest they're lying to you

principles.text: In startups there is no B+; aim for the A+ because anything less fails.
principles.quote: there's no you know a b is an F in startups pure like basically it's either an A plus or an f

principles.text: Great founders explain complex breakthroughs in very few words, since they must close customers, hires and money.
principles.quote: really really great Founders are able to communicate in very very few words these incredibly complex ideas

principles.text: In a hard fundraising market, aim for profitability or cash-flow break-even instead of relying on the next round.
principles.quote: the safest thing is try to get profitable
